headline: How octopuses squeeze through tiny holes

sources.title: How octopuses squeeze through teeny tiny holes (NPR)
How octopuses squeeze through too small gaps (The Company of Biologists, via EurekAlert!)
How do octopuses squeeze through tiny holes? (Popular Science)

chunks.text: Octopuses can [[squeeze]] their [[soft bodies]] through holes smaller than they are. A study published on November 5, 2026, shows how. Biologists in Austria and Italy {{teamed up}} with robot engineers in Singapore. They wanted to {{figure out}} the [[exact steps]] an octopus takes. The answer could help build robots for [[rescue work]] after earthquakes.

verbs.correct: To join others to do a task together
verbs.wrong: To win money for a new study
verbs.why: My brother and I team up for school projects. Two shops team up to sell food at the fair. Biologists in Austria and Italy teamed up with robot engineers in Singapore.

verbs.correct: To understand something by studying it
verbs.wrong: To share results with other scientists
verbs.why: My son figures out math problems very fast. Doctors try to figure out what causes the pain. The researchers wanted to figure out the exact steps an octopus takes.

chunks.text: The team tested two kinds of octopus, common and Mayan, at an aquarium in Vienna. An octopus is soft except for a small [[beak]] and a hard case around its brain. The [[distance]] between its eyes shows how wide that case is. The scientists built [[clear plastic]] boxes with holes and {{set up}} cameras. Some holes were wider than that, and some were smaller.

verbs.correct: To place equipment so it is ready
verbs.wrong: To check that equipment is safe
verbs.why: The band sets up its speakers before every show. My dad sets up the tent while we cook dinner. The scientists built clear plastic boxes with holes and set up cameras.

chunks.text: With a wide hole, common octopuses followed the same [[pattern]]. One arm went in first to {{check out}} the other side. More arms followed. In one last move, two arms [[gripped]] the wall with [[suckers]] and pulled the body across. With a smaller hole, a common octopus {{broke the last move down}} into two steps: other arms first, then the body. When the only hole was small, the Mayan octopuses {{stayed away}} and {{hung out}} in a [[corner]]. Offered two holes, they felt the small one, then {{gave up}} on it.

verbs.correct: To examine something to learn about it
verbs.wrong: To block an opening with something
verbs.why: Cats always check out a new box carefully. Buyers check out a house before they make an offer. First, one arm went into the hole to check out the other side.

verbs.correct: To divide something into smaller parts
verbs.why: Good teachers break big lessons down into small steps. She breaks her long run down into three parts. With a smaller hole, a common octopus broke the last move down into two steps.

verbs.wrong: To move slowly to the other side
verbs.why: Most deer stay away from busy roads. I stay away from that bridge when it rains. When the only hole was small, the Mayan octopuses stayed away.

verbs.wrong: To change color to match the walls
verbs.why: My kids hang out in the park after school. Our cat hangs out on the sofa all day. The Mayan octopuses hung out in a corner.

verbs.correct: To stop trying to do something
verbs.wrong: To make a hole bigger by pushing
verbs.why: Many people give up when a puzzle gets hard. My son never gives up on a difficult game. Offered two holes, the Mayan octopuses felt the small one, then gave up on it.

chunks.text: Most rescue robots are long and thin like snakes. That leaves little room for [[emergency supplies]] and [[sensors]], the parts that help a robot see and feel. An octopus-like robot could {{track down}} [[survivors]] under [[fallen buildings]] and {{drop off}} food and water. An engineer at the University of Connecticut, not part of the study, said the results {{back up}} the idea of robots that pull themselves forward instead of pushing. Robots usually {{take on}} [[dull]], dirty or dangerous jobs, he said. Octopuses suggest a new kind: [[delicate work]].

verbs.wrong: To send a signal for help
verbs.why: Police dogs track down people who are lost in the woods. Reporters track down people who saw the crash. An octopus-like robot could track down survivors under fallen buildings.
The mail carrier drops off packages every morning. Volunteers drop off meals at older people's homes. An octopus-like robot could also drop off food and water.

verbs.correct: To give support to an idea
verbs.wrong: To explain an idea in simple words
verbs.why: Good test results back up a doctor's idea. Photos often back up a witness's story. An engineer said the results back up the idea of robots that pull themselves forward instead of pushing.

verbs.correct: To agree to do a job
verbs.why: Our neighbor takes on extra work in the summer. Young workers often take on the hardest jobs. Robots usually take on dull, dirty or dangerous jobs, the engineer said.

mainIdea.s: Scientists filmed octopuses moving through holes smaller than their bodies and found repeated steps. They hope the findings will help engineers build better robots for disaster rescues.
mainIdea.why: The common octopuses used one arm to check out the hole and then followed set steps. The team wants robots that can track down survivors.

mainIdea.s: Researchers learned that both kinds of octopus fit through even the tiniest openings in exactly the same way. They believe any octopus can go wherever its hard brain case is able to pass.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the two kinds acted differently. The Mayan octopuses stayed away from a small hole and just hung out in a corner of the box.

mainIdea.s: A new aquarium in Vienna has opened a huge tank where visitors can watch octopuses hunt crabs. Officials expect thousands of families to visit it during the long winter school break.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a study on how octopuses squeeze through small holes. Researchers in Europe and Singapore teamed up to do it.

tf.s: Biologists and robotics researchers teamed up to study octopuses.
tf.why: Biologists in Austria and Italy worked with robotics researchers in Singapore.

tf.s: The common octopuses sent their bodies into the hole before their arms.
tf.why: One arm went into the hole first to check out the other side. The body came last.

tf.s: The Mayan octopuses stayed away from the smaller holes.
tf.why: They never touched a small hole on its own. With two holes, they gave up on the small one.

tf.s: The Mayan octopuses squeezed through every hole they were given.
tf.why: When a small hole was the only way out, they never touched it. They hung out in a corner.

tf.s: The researchers hope to build robots that can track down survivors.
tf.why: A robot that moves like an octopus could find people under fallen buildings after a disaster.

tf.s: Most rescue robots today are shaped like octopuses.
tf.why: Most rescue robots are long and thin like snakes. The team wants robots that can track down survivors in tight spaces.

lines.text: Did you see the study about octopuses and tiny holes?
I did. How do they even fit? It looks like [[a tight squeeze]].
Biologists in Europe and robot experts in Singapore {{teamed up}} to {{figure out}} the steps.
They {{set up}} cameras and filmed the octopuses in clear plastic boxes with holes.
And the octopus just tries to get to the other side?
First, one arm reaches into the hole to {{check out}} the other side. Then more arms follow and drag the body across.
That's smart. What about a really small hole?
The common octopus {{breaks the last move down}} into two steps. The other arms go first, then the body.
The Mayan octopuses {{stayed away}} from a small hole. They just {{hung out}} in a corner of the box.
Right. With two holes, they felt the small one first, then {{gave up}} and used the big one.
I guess you have to [[pick your battles]].
Engineers could [[learn a thing or two]] from them. A robot like that could {{track down}} survivors after an earthquake.
And {{drop off}} food and water, too?
That's the idea. One engineer says the results {{back up}} robots that pull themselves forward instead of pushing.
If it works, those robots could really [[save the day]].
